title: Command Line: Your Powerful Toolbox
description: Learn to direct your computer, move around your project, and run Python from the terminal.

lessons.title: Meet the terminal
lessons.content:
The terminal is a text-based way to give instructions to your computer. In VS Code, open it with Terminal > New Terminal.

A terminal runs a shell (such as Bash, zsh, or PowerShell). Python is a programming language that you can run from the shell. They are related tools, but they are not the same thing.

Try these safe commands in your own terminal:

pwd       Show the current folder (PowerShell also supports this)
ls        List files (PowerShell: dir)
python --version   Show the installed Python version (Windows may use py --version)

A command is made of a program and, sometimes, extra information called arguments. Press Enter to run it. Use the up-arrow key to revisit a previous command.
exercises: Write Python code that prints a friendly message. Download it as hello.py, then run it in your terminal with python hello.py (Windows: py hello.py).
Write Python code that prints the words you would use to ask the terminal which Python version is installed.
Write a short Python comment explaining the difference between the terminal and the Python language.

lessons.title: Move around your project
lessons.content:
Commands work in a current folder. Knowing where you are and how to move between folders helps you run the right files.

pwd       Show the current folder
ls        List files in this folder (PowerShell: dir)
cd folder-name   Move into a folder
cd ..     Move up one folder
mkdir practice   Create a folder named practice

Use ls (or dir) after moving to check where you are. These navigation commands are safe ways to explore. Be careful with commands you do not recognize, especially commands that delete or overwrite files.
exercises: Write a Python script that prints a three-step checklist for opening a project folder in the terminal.
Create a Python list of the commands pwd, ls, cd, and mkdir, then print each command on its own line.
Write a Python comment describing how cd .. changes the current folder.

lessons.title: Run Python from the terminal
lessons.content:
Save a Python program in a file ending in .py. In the terminal, move to the folder containing the file, then run it:

python hello.py

On many Windows installations, use py hello.py instead. Python can also run useful standard-library tools with the -m option, for example:

python -m unittest

If a command is unfamiliar, python --help shows Python's command options. This learning page runs your code inside your browser; use Download .py to save your solution before trying it in your own terminal.
exercises: Write a Python script that prints a message showing that your program ran successfully.
Write a Python script that prints the command you would use to run a file named practice.py.
Write a Python script that prints the command you would use to start Python's unittest test runner.

title: Python fundamentals
description: Start with values, variables, strings, numbers, input, and output.

lessons.title: First steps
lessons.content:
A variable gives a value a name. Python can store text, whole numbers, and decimal numbers.

Example:
name = "Ada"
age = 12
print(f"Hello, {name}! Next year you will be {age + 1}.")

The f before a string lets you put expressions inside braces.
exercises: Store your name and favorite hobby in variables and print a sentence.
Convert a distance from kilometers to miles (multiply by 0.621371).
Ask for a temperature in Celsius and print its Fahrenheit conversion.

title: Decisions and loops
description: Make choices with conditions and repeat work with loops.

lessons.title: Choose and repeat
exercises: Ask for an age and label the person as a child, teen, or adult.
Print numbers from 1 to 20 and label each even or odd.
Make a number guessing game with a fixed secret number.

title: Collections
description: Group related data with lists, dictionaries, sets, and tuples.

lessons.title: Grouping data
lessons.content:
Lists keep an ordered collection. Dictionaries associate keys with values. Sets keep unique values.

Example:
shopping = ["apples", "bread"]
shopping.append("tea")
scores = {"Ari": 8, "Bo": 10}
print(shopping)
print(scores["Ari"])
exercises: Make a shopping list, add and remove an item, then print each item.
Make a dictionary of names and phone numbers.
Count how often each word appears in a sentence.

title: Functions
description: Give reusable behavior a name and split problems into smaller steps.

lessons.title: Reusable behavior
lessons.content:
Functions accept inputs through parameters and can send a result back with return.

Example:
def rectangle_area(width, height):
    return width * height

area = rectangle_area(4, 3)
print(area)
exercises: Write a function that converts Celsius to Fahrenheit.
Write a function that returns the average of a list of numbers.
Split your guessing game into small functions with clear names.

title: Modules and errors
description: Reuse the standard library and handle invalid input clearly.

lessons.title: Imports and input validation
lessons.content:
An import gives you access to code from another module. Use try and except for errors you expect and know how to handle.

Example:
import random

print(random.randint(1, 6))

try:
    age = int(input("Age: "))
except ValueError:
    print("Please enter a whole number.")
exercises: Import math and calculate a circle's area.
Keep asking until the user enters a valid whole number.
Put a function in a separate file and import it.

title: Files and data
description: Read and write files, and save structured information as JSON or CSV.

lessons.title: Save and load data
lessons.content:
Pathlib provides convenient file paths. The json module converts between Python data and JSON text.

Example:
import json
from pathlib import Path

path = Path("progress.json")
path.write_text(json.dumps({"done": True}))
data = json.loads(path.read_text())
print(data)
exercises: Write a note to a text file, then read it back.
Save a list of completed lessons as JSON.
Read a CSV file with Python's csv module and summarize a column.

title: Testing
description: Check that your program behaves as expected with repeatable tests.

lessons.title: Test your code
lessons.content:
A test calls your code with known inputs and checks the result. Python includes unittest in its standard library.

Example:
import unittest

class AreaTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_rectangle(self):
        self.assertEqual(4 * 3, 12)

Run tests with: python -m unittest
exercises: Write tests for a temperature conversion function.
Test your shopping-list or guessing-game behavior.
Make one test fail by changing the code, then restore the correct behavior.
